# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

The methodology proceeds from diagnosis to supervised testing. It begins with a completed pilot (@sec-pilot) that identifies errors in fluent-only parsing, proceeds to corpus construction (@sec-data) that converts the formal account into paired supervision, and ends with a model experiment (@sec-model) comparing normalising and repair-aware targets.

## Pilot Study (Completed) {#sec-pilot}

The completed pilot tested whether a Gemma-2 9B semantic parser [@gemmateamGemma2Improving2024], fine-tuned with LoRA only on fluent sentence--SBN pairs [@huLoRALowRankAdaptation2021], could recover the fluent meaning from an input containing RSR. Following @senSemanticParsingDisfluent2021, the RSR variants changed only the natural-language input and were evaluated against the original fluent gold SBN. [Appendix A.1](#app-pilot-training) reports the pilot training configuration.

### Parsing Results and Output Diagnosis

The materials came from the English train-gold portion of PMB 5.1.0 [@abzianidzeParallelMeaningBank2017]. Because the source sentences and their fluent SBN targets were included in the LoRA fine-tuning data, the parser had been trained on the underlying fluent sentence--SBN mappings; only the RSR-modified inputs were new. Qwen3-32B [@yangQwen3TechnicalReport2025] selected a repair word and inserted a different word of the same part of speech immediately before it as the reparandum. The repair remained in place, keeping the intended meaning aligned with the fluent gold SBN. After three distinct variants were generated for each source and filtered, 833 sentences yielded 2,499 unmarked RSR inputs. Adding *I mean* between each reparandum and repair produced another 2,499. [Appendix A](#app-pilot-results) gives the full condition-level results.

Each output was converted into a graph and compared with the fluent reference SBN. The *scorable rate* records how many outputs could be converted and scored. For those outputs, SMATCH++ measures concept and relation overlap with the reference [@opitzSMATCHStandardizedExtended2023]. *Failure-penalised F1* assigns zero to unscoreable outputs before averaging, so graph-generation failures remain visible.

  Condition                    Scorable (%)   Failure-penalised F1
  -------------------------- -------------- ----------------------
  Fluent                               97.5          0.950$^{***}$
  Unmarked RSR                         94.6          0.786$^{***}$
  RSR + editing expression             76.5          0.609$^{***}$

  : Parser performance across the Fluent, unmarked-RSR and RSR-with-editing-expression input conditions. Asterisks indicate that all three pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons of failure-penalised F1 gave $p<.001$. {#tbl-pilot}

@tbl-pilot shows a stepwise decline in both measures. RSR lowered F1 while leaving most outputs scorable; adding *I mean* produced a further loss driven mainly by graph-generation failures. Among outputs that remained scorable, the additional decline in F1 was much smaller.

The output patterns point to a common source of this decline. The parser often mapped the words in the input into SBN without distinguishing their roles in the repair. Of the 2,363 scorable RSR outputs, 90.1% contained more concepts than the parser's output for the corresponding fluent source sentence, with a median of two additional concepts. Much of the fluent proposition therefore remained recoverable, but the reparandum was often added to the asserted content rather than interpreted as withdrawn.

Including *I mean* introduced further errors into this surface-based mapping. @fig-pilot-output shows a parse that recovers the accepted proposition about a cow giving birth, but also asserts the *goat* and interprets *I mean* as a meaning event involving the speaker. No structure records that the cow replaces the goat. The SBN is formally possible, but it does not express the intended RSR.

:::::: {.sbn-comparison #fig-pilot-output}
**Input:** A goat, I mean, a cow gave birth to a calf with two heads.

::::: {.sbn-panels}
:::: {.sbn-panel}
**Fluent reference SBN**

```{.sbn}
cow.n.01    % A cow
...
```
::::

:::: {.sbn-panel}
**RSR + editing-expression parse**

```{.sbn highlight-lines="1-4"}
goat.n.01    % A goat
person.n.01 EQU speaker      %I
mean.v.01 Theme -2 Agent -1 Time +1     % mean
time.n.08 EQU now
cow.n.01    % A cow
...
```
::::

:::::

Excerpts from the fluent reference and RSR parse. Highlighting marks content incorrectly asserted from the reparandum and editing expression; shared content is omitted.
::::::

The output still receives a SMATCH++ score of 0.764 because the accepted proposition continues to receive credit while the added content only lowers the overlap. A substantial graph score can therefore conceal the semantic error central to RSR. [Appendix A.5.1](#app-pilot-goat-cow) gives the complete RSR and fluent-input outputs.

### Recognition Probe and Implications

The parsing results do not show whether the model failed to recognise RSR or lacked an SBN pattern for representing it. I therefore removed the LoRA adapter and asked the instruction-tuned Gemma-2 9B to mark the reparandum, editing expression and repair in plain text. The probe detected 100.0% of inputs with an editing expression and 44.8% without one, while falsely identifying RSR in 1.0% of fluent inputs. The editing expression was therefore a strong cue, although detection did not ensure accurate segmentation.

The two surface forms exposed different weaknesses. Without an editing expression, the base model missed more than half of the RSRs, while the parser often folded both candidates into a fluent-looking graph. With *I mean*, the probe detected every RSR, but the parser often represented the expression as semantic content. Because the probe changed both the task and the adaptation state, it cannot isolate SBN generation as the source of error. The pilot also covered one model size and included no repair-aware supervision. The main experiment will therefore test repair-aware training across model sizes; the next section describes its targets.

## Repair-Aware Corpus Construction {#sec-data}

### Paired Construction

No existing corpus pairs replacement self-repair utterances with SBN targets that distinguish withdrawn from accepted content. The PMB contains fluent sentence--SBN pairs [@abzianidzeParallelMeaningBank2017], while speech and disfluency resources contain self-repairs without corresponding SBN annotations [@deshmukhResegmentationSWITCHBOARD1998; @passaliLARDLargescaleArtificial2022; @guptaDisflQABenchmarkDataset2021]. Each PMB source pair is therefore transformed in parallel into an RSR utterance and the repair-aware SBN defined in @sec-paired-configuration. Unlike the pilot, which altered only the utterance, this construction changes both sides of the pair.

@fig-paired-transformation summarises this parallel construction.

![Parallel construction of an RSR utterance and repair-aware target.](figures/paired-transformation.svg){#fig-paired-transformation width="760px" fig-alt="A square diagram: fluent sentence to RSR utterance by inserting a reparandum; fluent gold SBN to repair-aware SBN by RSR transformation; PMB gold links the fluent pair, and a dashed arrow marked with a question mark links the RSR pair."}

Construction will start from a fluent sentence, its fluent gold SBN and its word--concept alignment. An aligned noun, verb or adjective is selected as the repair, and a different expression of the same part of speech is drawn from WordNet [@millerWordNetLexicalDatabase1994] and inserted immediately before it. For example, *"She prefers tea"* becomes *"She prefers coffee, tea"*. The implemented corpus transformation replaces one aligned lexical concept at a time; the repair follows the inserted reparandum either immediately or after an intervening editing expression.

The repair keeps its gold representation. The transformation adds the reparandum in the paired `CORRECTION` and `CONJUNCTION` contexts, using the direct construction where possible and the anchor or movement construction where required. It preserves the source graph outside the selected replacement site. Each record stores the original and repair-aware SBNs, the two replacement concepts, their status, their links to shared content and the construction used. These fields pair each RSR input with either target in the model comparison and record the information needed to compute the structural scores in @sec-model. [Appendix E.6](#app-generated-record) shows a complete record.

### Validation and Selection

Structural validation checks that the target forms a well-defined graph, contains the paired RSR contexts, assigns withdrawn and accepted status correctly and preserves the source graph elsewhere. It also checks the links that connect both replacement concepts to shared content. A target that fails any check is excluded.

A legal graph can still contain a poor training example. The competing expressions must differ in meaning, yet both must fit the sentence context. Bidirectional NLI scores identify replacements that remain mutually entailing [@laurerLessAnnotatingMore2024], while a causal language model measures contextual fit as the mean token surprisal of the reparandum conditioned on its left context. The NLI boundaries and the upper surprisal threshold are set on a manually labelled calibration sample and frozen before the corpus is filtered. A separate sample from the retained data estimates the proportion that satisfies both criteria. [Appendix B](#app-corpus-selection) gives the calibration and audit procedure.

### Experimental Partitions

Every generated item inherits the train, development or test split of its PMB source document. All variants of a source remain together, preventing a training document from reappearing in evaluation. Every model condition also retains the same fluent PMB component. Two training conditions receive identical RSR utterances. The *normalising* condition pairs each utterance with its fluent gold SBN, whereas the *repair-aware* condition pairs it with the generated SBN that retains the replacement structure.

Every base RSR training item is retained without an editing expression. An additional marked variant is constructed for approximately 30% of base items using one of four editing expressions---*I mean*, *no*, *no wait* or *actually*---with the same SBN target. The current set contains 3,489 base items and 1,047 additional marked variants, for 4,536 RSR training rows; marked variants account for 23.1% of these rows. Thus training retains the fluent component, adds base RSR, and then adds marked variants. Selected items have greater row weight; the normalising and repair-aware conditions use identical inputs and sampling. Each test item contributes two matched utterances with the same repair content and target. One contains no editing expression, while the other contains one. The test expressions include both forms seen during training and the held-out *sorry*, allowing the effect of an editing expression and generalisation to an unseen expression to be evaluated separately.

Two test-only challenge sets contain adversarial examples that examine behaviour that positive, sentence-local RSR examples cannot establish. The non-RSR set contains lists, appositions and similar fluent sequences that exhibit local surface patterns resembling RSR without expressing replacement. It tests whether the parser distinguishes genuine repair from superficial similarity; assigning an RSR configuration to these items counts as a false positive. The discourse set contains controls without RSR, later reference to the accepted referent, reference to both replacement candidates and corrections between discourse turns. The last condition tests whether the within-clause configuration is applied outside its scope. [Appendix B](#app-corpus-selection) documents selection of these cases, and [Appendix D](#app-later-reference) gives a complete later-reference target.

### Feasibility and Scope

I have applied the implemented single-concept operator to all 9,552 English gold documents in the PMB training partition. @tbl-coverage-funnel shows the resulting structural yield before the non-RSR hold-out.

  Stage                                         Count   \% of lexical concepts
  ------------------------------------------ -------- ------------------------
  Lexical concepts (noun, verb, adjective)     23,232                    100.0
  Aligned to an uttered word                   17,886                     77.0
  Usable site with a WordNet reparandum        16,481                     70.9
  Structurally legal transformation            16,425                     70.7

  : Yield of the single-concept operator over the PMB training partition. Of the usable sites, 99.7% produce a legal transformation. {#tbl-coverage-funnel}

The 16,425 legal transformations form the candidate pool and include the direct, anchor and movement constructions defined in @sec-paired-configuration. Structural generation and validation are complete; linguistic filtering, the independent audit and final sampling remain. The sampling rule limits repeated use of a source document and is fixed before model training.

The main corpus covers immediate replacements of aligned noun, verb and adjective concepts. It does not include role, tense, aspect or delayed replacements. Its WordNet-derived reparanda and written PMB contexts also differ from spontaneous speech. The experiments will therefore test learnability within these boundaries, not coverage of naturally occurring RSR as a whole.

## Model Experiment {#sec-model}

The model experiment will test whether an LLM-based semantic parser can learn the repair-aware representation from @sec-data. A parse will count as successful only if it recovers the withdrawn and accepted content, assigns their status and links both to the surrounding clause. The evaluation will also test later reference, accepted meaning and generalisation beyond the training patterns.

### Experimental Design

The experiment will use instruction-tuned Qwen3.5 models at three parameter scales: 2B, 9B and 27B [@qwenQwen35Native2026]. Each model size will be trained under all three conditions, allowing the effect of the training target to be compared across model capacities.

All conditions will retain the fluent PMB pairs (@tbl-model-experiment). RSR normalisation will add the generated utterances with fluent gold SBN targets that omit the reparandum. Repair-aware training will use the same utterances with the repair-aware targets from @sec-paired-configuration.

  Training condition   RSR inputs   Target for RSR inputs         2B             9B            27B
  -------------------- ------------ ----------------------- -------------- -------------- --------------
  Fluent only          No           ---                      $\checkmark$   $\checkmark$   $\checkmark$
  RSR normalisation    Yes          Fluent gold SBN          $\checkmark$   $\checkmark$   $\checkmark$
  Repair-aware         Yes          Repair-aware SBN         $\checkmark$   $\checkmark$   $\checkmark$

  : Training conditions and model sizes. Every model size is trained under all three conditions with three matched random seeds. The two RSR conditions receive the same inputs and differ in the target assigned to each RSR item. {#tbl-model-experiment}

Within each model size, the normalising and repair-aware conditions have their inputs, example counts and training procedure held constant, so their comparison isolates the effect of retaining withdrawn content and its ordered replacement structure. The fluent-only condition provides a reference without RSR supervision, but its comparison with repair-aware training combines new examples and new targets. Results therefore pair gains in RSR representation with changes in accepted-meaning and fluent-input accuracy.

All conditions will use the same parsing instruction and LoRA adaptation procedure [@huLoRALowRankAdaptation2021]. The instruction does not identify an input as fluent or RSR-containing. Each model--condition combination will use three matched random seeds, giving 27 runs in total. Outputs will be evaluated without automatic output correction. [Appendix C.1](#app-model-config) specifies the full procedure.

### Evaluation

The primary measure is *RSR-structure accuracy*. An item is correct only if its output is a well-formed graph with the paired `CORRECTION`--`CONJUNCTION` structure. It must also assign the reparandum and repair to the withdrawn and accepted contexts and give both the required links to shared content. Component scores show which requirement failed. Graph validity and failure-penalised SMATCH++ are complementary measures of generation success and agreement with the complete target [@opitzSMATCHStandardizedExtended2023]. [Appendix C.2](#app-model-metrics) gives the metric definitions and a worked scoring example.

Two controls assess how repair-aware training affects accepted-meaning recovery and ordinary semantic parsing. For the automatically generated RSR items, the accepted content of each prediction is compared with the fluent gold PMB graph after RSR-specific structure is removed. This measures recovery of the speaker's final intention independently of success on the reparandum. The parsers are also evaluated on the unmodified PMB test partition. Its graph score measures ordinary semantic parsing, while the spurious-RSR rate records fluent inputs that are incorrectly assigned RSR structure.

The later-reference challenge set tests the main functional motivation for retaining withdrawn material. It checks links to the accepted referent, the withdrawn referent and both referents where the target requires them. At each model size, the normalising and repair-aware parsers are compared because only the latter is trained to retain the withdrawn referent and its discourse status.

Further tests examine whether the parser has learned an RSR distinction rather than a narrow surface pattern. Paired versions of each test item measure the effect of an editing expression while holding its lexical content constant, and *sorry* tests a marker excluded from training. The non-RSR set measures false alarms on lists, appositions and coordination. Cross-turn corrections test whether the within-clause configuration is applied outside its intended scope.

The error diagnosis distinguishes failures of RSR structure, status and semantic-role attachment from representations of editing expressions, spurious RSR analyses and malformed SBN. Statistical comparisons use the original PMB source document as the unit of observation, with its variants aggregated before testing. For each model size, the three matched seeds are compared separately and their mean difference and range are reported; a result is treated as stable only when its direction is consistent across seeds. [Appendix C.5](#app-model-statistics) records the full error scheme and statistical procedure.
